\begin{center}
    \Large
    \textbf{Abstract}
\end{center}

We examine how gross administrative spending per resident changed after Norway’s 2020 municipal mergers. We construct geographically consistent accounts for 20 merger units and 285 controls from 2015 to 2025. The difference-in-differences estimate is NOK 2,238 lower annual spending per resident relative to all controls and NOK 1,132 lower relative to controls in the treated population range. Spending in merged areas fell from its 2019 peak through 2022. After 2022 the gap widened mainly because control spending continued to rise. Faster pre-merger spending growth in the treated group limits how much of the difference can be attributed to consolidation.

\newpage

```{r build-panel}
#| include: false
sample_units$treated <- as.integer(grepl(" ", sample_units$y2019))
raw_codes <- substr(panel$region, 1, 4)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(raw_codes), all(grepl("^[0-9]{4}$", raw_codes)))
raw_names <- sub("^[0-9]{4} +", "", panel$region)
sample_units$municipality <- raw_names[match(sample_units$y2024, raw_codes)]
stopifnot(!anyNA(sample_units$municipality))

aggregate_year <- function(year) {
  period <- as.character(cut(year, breaks = c(2014, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2023, 2025),
                             labels = c("y2015", "y2017", "y2018", "y2019", "id", "y2024")))
  members <- strsplit(sample_units[[period]], " ", fixed = TRUE)
  codes <- unlist(members, use.names = FALSE)
  stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(codes), all(codes %in% raw_codes))
  cost_col <- paste("Beløp (1000 kr) 120 Administrasjon",
                    "Brutto driftsutgifter på funksjon/tjenesteområde", year)
  pop_col <- paste("Personer (antall)", year, "I alt")
  stopifnot(all(c(cost_col, pop_col) %in% names(panel)))
  rows <- lapply(members, match, table = raw_codes)
  # A missing constituent makes the corresponding total missing.
  sum_members <- function(column) {
    vapply(rows, function(i) sum(panel[[column]][i]), numeric(1))
  }
  cost <- sum_members(cost_col)
  population <- sum_members(pop_col)
  stopifnot(all(population > 0, na.rm = TRUE))
  data.frame(
    id = sample_units$id, municipality = sample_units$municipality, year = year,
    treated = sample_units$treated, post = as.integer(year >= 2020),
    did = sample_units$treated * as.integer(year >= 2020), event_time = year - 2020L,
    admin_1000nok = cost, population = population,
    admin_nok_pc = 1000 * cost / population,
    source_codes = sample_units[[period]]
  )
}

panel_all <- do.call(rbind, lapply(2015:2025, aggregate_year))
# Keep all usable municipality-years. Missing values never become zero.
df_did <- subset(panel_all, !is.na(admin_nok_pc))
df_did <- df_did[order(df_did$id, df_did$year), ]
row.names(df_did) <- NULL
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(df_did[c("id", "year")]))

stopifnot(nrow(df_did) == 3352L, sum(sample_units$treated) == 20L)
data_dir <- "dokumentobjekter/data"
dir.create(data_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
openxlsx::write.xlsx(list(panel_data = df_did),
                     file.path(data_dir, "final_data.xlsx"), overwrite = TRUE)
```

```{r estimate-models}
#| include: false
fmt <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
base_pop <- filter(df_did, year == 2015)
limits <- range(base_pop$population[base_pop$treated == 1])
size_ids <- filter(base_pop, between(population, limits[1], limits[2]))$id
restricted <- filter(df_did, id %in% size_ids)

estimate_did <- function(data) {
  fixest::feols(admin_nok_pc ~ did | id + year, data = data, vcov = ~id)
}
estimate_slope <- function(data) {
  pre <- mutate(filter(data, year < 2020), trend = treated * (year - 2015))
  fixest::feols(admin_nok_pc ~ trend | id + year, data = pre, vcov = ~id)
}
model <- estimate_did(df_did)
model_no_2019 <- estimate_did(filter(df_did, year != 2019))
model_size <- estimate_did(restricted)
slope_all <- estimate_slope(df_did)
slope_size <- estimate_slope(restricted)
```

# Introduction

When Moss and Rygge merged in January 2020, the new municipality inherited two administrations and the population both had served. Combining the accounts alone could produce no saving. A saving would require some change in how the work was done, such as replacing two payroll arrangements with one. Yet the first financial consequence of combining them might be the expense of moving staff and records to a common system. For a council considering a merger, the relevant budget question concerns both the size of any saving and when it might appear.

Norway's municipal reform began in 2014. Its objectives included financially sustainable municipalities, local capacity and the quality of services. Central government offered merger subsidies to help finance the transition [@askim2025local]. A grant could cover part of the cost to the local budget while the expenditure itself would still appear in the gross spending measure used here. The main wave of mergers took effect on 1 January 2020, when the number of municipalities fell from 422 to 356. Decisions and preparations preceded that date by several years [@askim2025local]. This timing gives us a common implementation year across the mergers studied here, but makes the last pre-merger budgets particularly important to the comparison.

We ask how gross administrative spending per resident changed in the municipalities that merged in 2020 relative to municipalities with stable boundaries. We follow the same geographical areas from 2015 through 2025. Six years of post-merger accounts allow us to distinguish an initial fall in spending from a gap that widens because spending elsewhere continues to rise. These patterns have different implications for what a council could reasonably expect to see in its own accounts.

# Literature review

The 2007 Danish municipal reform provides a close comparison. @blom2014size find that amalgamation reduced administrative costs per inhabitant. Their outcome captures a function for which several councils may previously have paid separately. Extending the analysis to other spending categories, @blom2016jurisdiction find that savings in some areas were offset by increases elsewhere. An administrative saving can therefore coexist with an unchanged total budget. For example, a municipality could use the resources released from administration to increase spending on services. Our choice of outcome follows the first Danish study, while the second limits the budgetary conclusion we can draw from it.

The Norwegian evidence suggests a further reason to look at the years surrounding implementation. @askim2025local examine whether municipalities committed additional resources before their budgets were combined. Smaller merger partners showed particularly strong pre-merger overspending on current expenditure. Their evidence concerns wider spending categories than the administrative accounts examined here. It nevertheless gives a specific reason to question whether expenditure immediately before the merger represents an ordinary year for the future partners. A comparison beginning in 2019 could pick up the reversal of unusually high spending as well as any economies achieved by combining administrations.

# Theoretical framework

## Fixed costs and the scope for savings

Consider a municipality serving $N$ residents with annual administrative expenditure $F+vN$. Here $F$ is the cost of maintaining one administrative organisation and $v$ is the cost of work that rises in proportion to population. Average expenditure is $F/N+v$. Suppose two municipalities with populations $N_1$ and $N_2$ each incur the same fixed cost. Across their combined territory they initially spend $2F/(N_1+N_2)+v$ per resident. If one administration can serve both territories at the same variable cost, the potential annual saving per resident is $F/(N_1+N_2)$. This simple example expresses the scale argument examined by @blom2014size and clarifies why a merger on paper cannot by itself generate the predicted saving.

The size of the saving depends on which tasks can actually be combined. One financial director may oversee the consolidated accounts, while the staff processing invoices still face roughly the same volume of work. A geographically dispersed municipality might also retain local offices or incur extra coordination costs. In the example, either retaining part of the second fixed cost or increasing the cost per transaction reduces the gain. A municipality could even spend the same amount while acquiring specialist capacity that its predecessors could not afford individually. Expenditure alone therefore gives an incomplete measure of what the administration produces.

## Preparation and adjustment

Two mechanisms can change the path of spending around implementation. First, integration requires work. Migrating payroll records, agreeing on contracts and training staff can raise expenditure before the old systems are retired. The Norwegian Generalist Municipality Commission reports that administrative costs have tended to rise temporarily around mergers ([NOU 2023:9, section 15.1](https://www.regjeringen.no/no/dokumenter/nou-2023-9/id2968517/?ch=6)). Second, a predecessor council may approve spending whose benefits accrue locally while part of the future cost falls on residents of its merger partners. This common-pool incentive underlies the analysis in @askim2025local. Both mechanisms can raise pre-merger expenditure, although only the second requires a council to shift costs onto others.

These mechanisms yield two expectations for the accounts. Recurring savings should become visible once duplicated functions have been removed. A temporary preparation cost should disappear even if the recurring cost of administration does not change. Both can produce a decline after a pre-merger peak. We therefore compare several pre-merger years, inspect the annual paths, and repeat the estimate without 2019. The accounts identify neither the purpose of each transaction nor which council initiated it, so those checks speak to timing rather than to the motives of individual councils.

# Data

## Sources and geographical units

We combine annual gross operating expenditure on administration, KOSTRA function 120, from Statistics Norway's municipal consolidated accounts with population on 31 December. Expenditure is reported in thousands of current NOK. The analysis covers five fiscal years before implementation and six afterwards. The sources are [SSB table 12362](https://www.ssb.no/en/statbank/table/12362) and [SSB table 11805](https://www.ssb.no/en/statbank/table/11805).

The unit of observation is a municipality on consistent boundaries in a given year. For Moss, using only old Moss before 2020 would omit both Rygge's spending and the people it served. Instead, we sum both predecessors' expenditure, sum their populations and divide the first total, converted to NOK, by the second. The resulting pre-merger series describes the territory served by the new Moss. It gives each predecessor's residents the appropriate weight even when one predecessor is much smaller than the other. Taking a simple mean of their per-resident spending would give both administrations equal influence over the result.

We use the 2020 municipality code as a stable identifier and map earlier and later reporting codes back to it. A change of code alone does not count as a merger. A transfer of part of a municipality presents a different problem because the accounts do not indicate what share of spending belongs to the transferred territory. Starting from 356 geographical units, the crosswalk excludes 51 for boundary or accounting reasons, including partial transfers, earlier changes affecting comparability and Oslo's accounting exception. The retained sample comprises 20 merger units and 285 controls. The appendix documents the mapping used in the analysis.

## Measurement and sample coverage

```{=tex}
\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Variables used in the difference-in-differences analysis}
\label{tab:did-variables}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}lX@{}}
\hline
\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Definition} \\
\hline
Administrative spending ($Y_{it}$)
  & Annual gross operating expenditure on administration
    (KOSTRA function 120), in current NOK per resident.
    Calculated as $1{,}000$ times total expenditure in thousand NOK
    divided by the number of residents in municipality $i$ in year $t$. \\[4pt]
Treated ($D_i$)
  & Equals 1 in every year for municipalities that merged on
    1 January 2020, and 0 for control municipalities. \\[4pt]
Post ($P_t$)
  & Equals 1 in 2020--2025 and 0 in 2015--2019, for both groups. \\[4pt]
DiD ($D_i \times P_t$)
  & Equals 1 for merged municipalities from 2020 onward,
    and 0 for all other municipality-year observations. \\
\hline
\end{tabularx}

\smallskip
\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
\footnotesize
\textit{Note.} Before a merger, expenditure and population are each
summed across the predecessor municipalities before calculating spending
per resident. Each municipality-year receives equal weight in the
regression. Expenditure and population come from Statistics Norway
tables 12362 and 11805, respectively.
\end{minipage}
\end{table}
```

All 20 merger units contribute observations in every year. Three control municipalities, Nesna, Træna and Evenes, lack spending observations in 2019. We leave those municipality-years out, yielding 3,352 usable observations from a possible 3,355. Replacing missing amounts with zero would artificially lower the control mean in precisely the year most relevant to the anticipation check. The descriptive figure uses the available observations in each year, and the fixed-effects regression uses the same data.

Population plays two distinct roles. Within a merger it determines each predecessor's contribution to spending per resident. Across municipalities, each observed municipality-year receives equal weight in the regression. A change of NOK 100 per resident in a small municipality therefore matters as much to the coefficient as the same change in a large one. This weighting suits a question about the experience of the average municipality. A national budget calculation would also need the populations affected and the individual spending changes across those populations.

# Methods

## Comparison and identification

Our difference-in-differences (DiD) design compares the change in the 20 merger units with the contemporaneous change in controls. A before-and-after comparison confined to merged areas would also capture rising wages and other changes in the cost of running local government. Controls provide a benchmark for those developments. All treated units entered the reform in the same year, so none serves as a control for a later merger. We estimate

$$
Y_{it}=\alpha_i+\lambda_t+\beta(D_i\times P_t)+\varepsilon_{it},
$$

where $Y_{it}$ is annual administrative spending in current NOK per resident. Municipality fixed effects absorb persistent differences in spending levels. Year fixed effects absorb annual changes common to both groups in NOK per resident. The two sets of effects also absorb the separate treatment and post indicators. The coefficient $\beta$ summarises the relative change across the six post-merger years. We cluster standard errors by municipality because a spending shock can persist across several budgets of the same municipality.

A causal interpretation requires a credible path for spending in merged territories had the administrations remained separate. Parallel trends means that their average spending would have changed by the same amount as in controls in that counterfactual. The groups can start at different levels. A second requirement concerns anticipation. If merger preparations already increased spending in the baseline years, the estimated change compares the new organisation with administrations that were already responding to the decision. The timing of the decision and implementation matters even though the legal merger date is unambiguous. For the assumptions behind this interpretation, see [Roth et al. (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2023.03.008).

## Assessing the comparison group

The median population in 2015 was 22,232 in the future merger units and 3,903 in controls. This gap matters because a fixed administrative expense translates into a much larger amount per resident in a small municipality. Even a common percentage increase in that expense can produce different increases in NOK per resident. Municipality fixed effects absorb the initial level difference, but they cannot absorb a difference in subsequent growth. We therefore repeat the model using only controls inside the merger units' 2015 population range. Using population measured before implementation avoids selecting controls according to how they developed afterwards.

We also use the five pre-merger observations per treated unit to estimate a separate linear trend diagnostic. On the pre-2020 sample we replace the DiD interaction with the interaction of treatment status and years since 2015, retaining municipality and year effects. Its coefficient gives the difference in annual spending growth between groups, in NOK per resident per year. We estimate this slope for both control groups. It is a summary of the available pre-period and does not assume the same slope difference would have continued after 2020.

# Results

```{r fig-spending}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Mean annual administrative spending per resident. Each municipality receives equal weight. The vertical line marks the transition to the post-merger period."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.7
means <- function(data, series) {
  data |>
    group_by(year) |>
    summarise(spending = mean(admin_nok_pc), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(series = series)
}
annual <- bind_rows(
  means(filter(df_did, treated == 1), "Merged in 2020"),
  means(filter(df_did, treated == 0), "All controls"),
  means(filter(restricted, treated == 0), "Population-range controls")
)
ggplot(annual, aes(year, spending, colour = series, linetype = series)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2019.5, colour = "grey65", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("All controls" = "#346398",
    "Merged in 2020" = "#993D64", "Population-range controls" = "#28735A")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2025) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Current NOK per resident", colour = NULL,
       linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Annual spending and pre-merger trends

In 2015, the future merger units spent an average of NOK 4,450 per resident, compared with NOK 6,045 in all controls. By 2019 the means had risen to NOK 6,384 and NOK 7,181 respectively. Much of the narrowing occurred near implementation. Between 2017 and 2019 annual spending rose by about NOK 1,470 per resident in the merger group, compared with NOK 639 in controls. For the merger group relative to all controls in @fig-spending, the estimated pre-merger slope difference is positive, at NOK `r fmt(coef(slope_all)[1])` per resident per year (95% confidence interval `r fmt(confint(slope_all)[1, 1])` to `r fmt(confint(slope_all)[1, 2])`). The full control group therefore provides a questionable benchmark for the trajectory of spending even before the municipalities formally merged.

After implementation the merger group fell to NOK 5,158 in 2022, then rose to NOK 5,434 in 2025. Controls reached NOK 8,525 in 2022 and NOK 10,719 in 2025. The distinction between these two intervals matters. From 2019 to 2022 the gap widened because spending fell in merged territories while it rose in controls. From 2022 to 2025 spending increased in both groups. The additional widening in those later years came predominantly from growth among controls. A widening gap at the end of the series consequently cannot be read as a fresh budget cut in the merged municipalities each year.

## Pooled estimates and sensitivity checks

```{r results-table}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
column <- function(model) {
  interval <- confint(model, level = 0.95)
  c(fmt(coef(model)[1]), fmt(sqrt(vcov(model)[1, 1])),
    paste0("[", fmt(interval[1, 1]), ", ", fmt(interval[1, 2]), "]"),
    fmt(nobs(model)))
}
results <- data.frame(
  Measure = c("Merged × Post", "Clustered SE", "95% confidence interval",
              "Observations"),
  Baseline = column(model), `Omit 2019` = column(model_no_2019),
  `Population range` = column(model_size), check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(results, format = "latex", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
  caption = "Relative change in annual administrative spending (NOK per resident).")
```

The baseline estimate is a relative decline of NOK 2,238 per resident per year. Its municipality-clustered 95% confidence interval runs from NOK `r fmt(confint(model)[1, 1])` to NOK `r fmt(confint(model)[1, 2])` per resident. The magnitude may seem surprising given that the treated mean in 2025 exceeded its 2015 level. The regression compares changes between groups and pools several years on either side. It is entirely possible for a municipality to spend more than it did a decade earlier while spending considerably less than the comparison trend would predict. The interval measures sampling uncertainty conditional on the specification. Its width does not resolve the uncertainty about the comparison trend.

Omitting 2019 removes 302 observations and reduces the estimated relative decline to NOK 2,102, about 6% below the baseline in absolute terms. Thus the high treated mean in the final pre-merger year contributes to the size of the estimate, but that single year cannot account for the result. Preparations spanning several budgets could still influence the remaining pre-period. Dropping 2019 also does nothing to alter the strong subsequent growth among controls.

Restricting controls to the treated population range of 2,672 to 193,420 retains all 20 mergers and 176 controls. Of the 109 controls removed, 108 were below the lower bound. The estimated decline falls to NOK 1,132, roughly half the baseline magnitude. In 2015 these retained controls spent NOK 4,241 per resident, much closer to the merger group's NOK 4,450. Yet their mean reached only NOK 4,944 by 2019. The estimated pre-period slope difference actually rises to NOK `r fmt(coef(slope_size)[1])` per resident per year. Similar initial spending and overlapping populations thus solve only part of the comparison problem. Neither estimate offers a clean basis for choosing a single figure for merger savings.

# Discussion and conclusion

The results are consistent with an administrative saving, particularly during the first years in which the new municipalities operated. They are also consistent with the unwinding of spending incurred during preparation. The stronger evidence concerns the spending path itself. Administrative expenditure in the merged territories fell after its 2019 peak and then stabilised within a relatively narrow range in nominal terms. How much of the later gap we attribute to the mergers depends heavily on what we believe would otherwise have happened in those territories. Removing mostly small controls changes that benchmark substantially.

For a council preparing a merger budget, the distinction affects which savings can credibly be entered into a financial plan. A council can identify the annual cost of a contract it expects to retire, the date on which it can terminate that contract, and the one-off cost of moving to the replacement system. Those figures can be checked against subsequent accounts. Applying the national comparison coefficient to the local population would bypass those questions and give a misleading impression of precision. It would also treat the full post-merger gap as cash released for other purposes, even in years when the council's own expenditure increased.

Two limits qualify the wider policy interpretation. First, the design covers mergers whose predecessor accounts can be combined for the same territory. Municipalities that absorbed only part of a neighbour may have faced different integration costs. Second, function 120 records gross expenditure in current prices. It cannot distinguish lower input use from changes in the allocation of staff time across accounting functions, and it gives no direct evidence on administrative output. Combining expenditure data with staffing, case-processing times or service access would help establish what residents received for the money spent.

For the 20 mergers studied here, both comparison groups imply lower relative administrative expenditure after 2020. The smaller estimate obtained with population-comparable controls and the divergence already visible before implementation limit the causal conclusion. The evidence supports following merger budgets across several years and examining which recurring costs actually disappear before treating the observed difference as a permanent efficiency gain.

## R code {.unnumbered}

The analysis starts from the joined SSB expenditure and population extracts. The code uses a local copy of that file when available and otherwise downloads it from the project repository. Municipality codes are stored as character strings to preserve leading zeros. The resulting workbook contains the municipality-years used in the baseline regression.

### Prepare the source extracts {.unnumbered}

To rebuild the joined input from the original Statbank downloads, place the two semicolon-delimited extracts in the data directory and run the following preparation step once.

```{r, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
read_extract <- function(filename) {
  readr::read_delim(file.path("dokumentobjekter/data", filename),
    delim = ";", skip = 1, locale = readr::locale(encoding = "Windows-1252"),
    na = c(".", ":", "..", ""), show_col_types = FALSE)
}
costs <- read_extract("administrative_costs.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(!region %in% c("EAK Landet", "EAKUO Landet uten Oslo"))
population <- read_extract("personer_kommuner.csv")
joined <- dplyr::left_join(costs, population, by = "region",
                           relationship = "one-to-one")
readr::write_csv(joined, "dokumentobjekter/data/panel.csv", na = "")
```
